outcome: No result was found addressing whether a prime can be simultaneously a Wieferich prime base 2 (2^(p-1) ≡ 1 mod p²) and base 3 (3^(p-1) ≡ 1 mod p²); the question remains open with no theoretical or computational progress specific to it since 26 January 2024.
summary: This bullet asks whether a single prime p can satisfy both 2^(p-1) ≡ 1 (mod p²) (Wieferich prime base 2) and 3^(p-1) ≡ 1 (mod p²) (Wieferich prime base 3, a.k.a. Mirimanoff prime) simultaneously. As of the frozen revision, the only known base-2 Wieferich primes are 1093 and 3511, and the only known base-3 ones are 11 and 1006003, with no overlap, and a computational 'arms race' (culminating in PrimeGrid's completed search to 2^64, finished December 2022 — before the window) established that no such simultaneous prime exists below that bound. I searched extensively for any development since 26 January 2024: (1) whether PrimeGrid or another distributed-computing project extended the search bound past 2^64 — no such project was found; PrimeGrid's Wieferich search appears dormant since December 2022, and no new bound announcement was found; (2) whether any theoretical paper proved existence, non-existence, or any partial result narrowing this specific simultaneity question — none was found; recent arXiv papers on Wieferich primes (Wieferich primes in number fields, Aug 2025; Wieferich primes for Drinfeld modules, Dec 2024; Wieferich and Mersenne primes for function fields, Dec 2025; Wieferich Primes and Monogenic Trinomials, May 2026) all concern generalizations to other algebraic settings (number fields, function fields, Drinfeld modules) or unrelated applications (monogenic trinomials), not the base-2/base-3 simultaneity question over the rationals; (3) whether any AI system (e.g., DeepMind's Gemini survey of Erdős problems, Feb 2026) touched this specific question — I found that a related but distinct object, 'double Wieferich prime pairs' (pairs of distinct primes p,q with p^(q-1)≡1 mod q² and q^(p-1)≡1 mod p²), has known examples, but this is a different concept (two different primes in a mutual relation, not one prime being Wieferich in two different fixed bases) and is not a case or variant relevant to this bullet. I also found that a Google DeepMind Gemini audit of Erdős problems surfaced an issue in the formal-conjectures repository concerning a *different* problem (Erdős-11, on whether non-Wieferich primes base 2 are infinite, via Granville–Soundararajan), and a related Erdős conjecture (Dupuy–Weirich, on digits of powers of 2 in base 3) connects both Wieferich bases 2 and 3 to a different question (digit patterns), not to simultaneity of one prime satisfying both congruences. None of this constitutes progress on, or AI involvement in, the specific problem stated in this bullet. I conclude the correct classification is 'open' with no change found.
competing_reading: None of the tangential results (double Wieferich pairs, Wieferich primes in number fields/function fields/Drinfeld modules, the Dupuy–Weirich digit conjecture) plausibly count even as a 'case' of this problem under §3.1, since they change the objects or question rather than restricting the stated one; I do not think a different classification is defensible here.
what_would_settle_it: Either (a) a proof that no prime can satisfy both congruences simultaneously, (b) discovery of an explicit prime satisfying both (which would also require it to individually be a Wieferich prime in each base, which is itself extremely rare), or (c) a new distributed-computing project extending the joint search bound past 2^64, which would be `progress` even though the question itself would remain open.
